title: Netflix’s Indian summer
body_text: The days of playing a housekeeper at the Airbnb you already paid a cleaning fee for are over. As part of a new global policy effective Nov. 20, Airbnb hosts will not be able to ask guests to do chores that require “significant effort” such as taking out the trash, stripping the sheets, or washing dishes. Hosts can still ask guests to leave dishes in the sink or, say, leave the trash in a bear-proof container when staying in a cabin, but Airbnb has finally drawn the line between being a considerate guest and working for your keep, after already paying for it. Stocks had a particularly rough day on Thursday, with the S&P 500 falling 1.2% and the Nasdaq 100 dropping 2.6%, marking the tech-heavy index’s worst day since June. Despite posting a relatively strong third quarter where earnings came in above expectations and revenue landed roughly in line with estimates, Netflix has been sent lower this week after the streamer set a new Q4 sales forecast that was slimmer than Wall Street expected and tempered ad revenue estimates. One silver lining among the clouds looming over the company from its Q3 report? India, which got six shoutouts in Netflix’s latest letter to shareholders; double the amount of references to the “US” or “United States.” Clearly the streamer has something to shout about in the Indian market, which sits in what is — currently, at least — the smallest global region for Netflix. India sits in the company’s Asia Pacific region, which accounted for just $1.54 billion of its total $12.88 billion revenue figure from the third quarter. Still, the APAC segment’s position could change if the success in India continues, with Netflix adding more net paid subscribers in the nation than ever before, revenues rising 18%, and view hours up 24% from the same period last year. The streamer highlighted “Lock Upp,” its first daily reality TV show, as a standout success in India, driving “the most viewing of any title on Netflix” in the country ever. Scripted hits like “Operation Safed Sagar” and “Musafir Cafe” also contributed to growth, as the company itself downsizes at a faster pace than it has since 2022. Doing better in the most populous nation in the world, which per the World Bank’s reckonings also still boasts one of the fastest growing major global economies, is obviously a boon for the world’s biggest film and TV streaming service. However, with at least some of the growth undoubtedly down to a generous tie-in with Indian e-commerce giant Flipkart — customers can get a free monthly Netflix Mobile subscription by spending ₹299 (~$3.15) on four individual orders in a single month — it might be a little early to put too much stock in the advance for now. According to the latest installment of an infrequent Gallup survey of US adults (the first since 2022), fewer of us are heading out to shop for groceries, eating out in restaurants, and even ordering takeout food, as the way Americans live week-to-week continues to shift. Gallup noted that Americans are tending to spread their weekly grocery trips out a little further, while also highlighting the rise of online staple shopping, with 15% of Americans now doing a weekly grocery order online compared to just 4% less than 10 years ago. Dining out and ordering takeout, despite the cursed online discourse around how it can sometimes work out cheaper than eating at home, have both declined of late. A still stunning — to this writer, at least — 4% of Americans still report that they never eat out at a restaurant. That — or 278 billion kroner, to be more accurate — is how much Norway’s sovereign wealth fund lost over the last quarter, the company that manages the fund announced yesterday . The loss was mostly owing to just how much of the world’s largest wealth fund’s fixed income portfolio is wrapped up in government bonds, with 70% allocated to the interest rate-hit investments. Staggeringly, shedding $30 billion doesn’t actually put too much of a dent in the Norwegian wealth fund, which is still worth around $2.3 trillion, shedding the rough equivalent of an Adidas ($31.5B), 7-Eleven ($30.5B), or Reddit ($29.5B) in a single quarter still has to sting. Apple’s iPhone Duo, which folds out to the size of a small iPad, is “a messy, expensive, good time,” according to The Verge . A combined SpaceX - Tesla may become subject to the “conglomerate discount” –– when a complex company with many diversified revenue streams becomes difficult for investors to size up, resulting in a lower valuation –– per Business Insider . Meta’s board created a new class of shares so CEO Mark Zuckerberg could sell his shares to pay a proposed California wealth tax without losing his control of the company .

title: 👀 Wall Street gets a peak inside Anthropic
body_text: The Los Angeles Dodgers were favorites to win this year’s World Series. And when they were surprisingly swept by the Milwaukee Brewers, it wasn’t just the team that lost – businesses around Dodger stadium also saw potential revenue evaporate. Fortune reports that a restaurant group that runs bars near the stadium prepared for exactly that possibility by placing a $60,000 trade on Kalshi that the Dodgers would not advance. The trade, which doubled in value after LA’s playoff exit, helped to fill the hole in the group’s revenue from all the Dodger’s fans who now won’t be packing bars before or during World Series games. Investors have been eager to peek under the hood of Anthropic ahead of its anticipated Wall Street debut, which could value the AI company at around $2 trillion. The Wall Street Journal got their hands on an early draft of Anthropic’s hotly anticipated S-1 , which paints a picture of a company with surging revenues but also sky-high compute costs and a medley of risk factors. Here are some highlights : Revenue is growing at an impressive rate: It reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of this year, up from $1.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. They are also spending a ton of money on compute. The company spent $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, up from $2.3 billion spent on infrastructure during the same period in 2025. The company already agreed to pay $450 billion in cloud computing agreements over the next seven to ten years and it can’t back out of those. It warned it could potentially spend $750 billion “in the coming years,” per the Journal. It is in the red. The company reported a net loss of $80 billion during the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion a year earlier. Most of that loss is accounting charges; it still reported operating loss in H1 2026 but it was lower than the year before. Anthropic makes it very clear that it sees AI as a risky business. According to the Journal, “roughly a third” of the draft prospectus was dedicated to risk factors ranging from liability tied to potential data security incidents, models “blackmailing” people to the political risk tied to the backlash against data centers. The CEO isn’t getting a Musk-sized pay day. Dario Amodei’s total compensation is $18 million, which is in line with the median pay for S&P 500 companies but less than many of his Big Tech peers. Anthropic’s numbers scooped by the Journal give a rare glimpse at the precise economics of running an AI company. The good news is Anthropic’s revenue, as of June 30, is growing faster than its costs. The bad news is that its costs are really high. Anthropic needs to convince investors that its revenues are going to keep growing faster than its enormous spending commitments. But, as Bloomberg’s Parmy Olson recently pointed out , the price of building AI models keeps going up while the price tag on AI products keeps going down. Anthropic can't guarantee that its revenue will keep soaring, but it's already committed to paying hundreds of billions of dollars for computing power. “That doesn’t necessarily mean a bursting bubble, but it does look like the real power increasingly lies with the companies that distribute and power the technology: cloud giants like Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon .com Inc.,” Olson wrote. Amazon’s annual holiday hiring surge is set to be bigger than ever, the e-commerce giant has announced . The company says it will hire over 300,000 seasonal, part-time, and full-time new employees to deal with the increase in orders it sees during the holiday shopping season. The yield on 10-year French government bonds hit 5% on Wednesday , as the nation’s borrowing costs spiked amid mass unrest that has turned violent at times. Larry Ellison went on a borrowing spree to fund his son’s takeover of Warner Bros ., the Wall Street Journal reports . Wall Street stock strategists have a new favorite word . The average US mortgage rate fell for the first time in 2 months, dropping to 7.41% from 7.5% . Coca-Cola bought Costa coffee for $5 billion, hoping to create a global self-serve coffee behemoth. It didn’t end up that way, Bloomberg reports , largely because espresso machines are more complex than soda vending machines. Wearing a necktie can decrease blood flow to the brain by as much as 7.5%, a 2018 study found. Lockheed Martin , TTM Technologies , and Procter & Gamble slated to release earnings ahead of the open. Postmarket earnings due out from Western Digital , Bloom Energy , and Comfort Systems USA .

title: 🤖 Meta has billions riding on its Muse
body_text: Usually you want a taco that has some varying texture. A woman in Texas is suing a regional taco chain, Torchy’s Tacos, for $250,000 after nearly swallowing a cow tooth. It’s not an uncommon thing to find in barbacoa, the kind of meat that filled her “Democrat” taco, which is slow cooked beef cheek. Still, the woman was “grossed out and sickened,” according to reports. Meta — one of the largest and spendiest companies in the artificial intelligence trade — is slated to report earnings today after the bell. The report comes at a time when investors are increasingly worried about the amount of debt companies are taking on to fuel their AI ambitions. Specifically, investors are worried that companies like Meta took on a dangerous amount of debt to create products that have not yet proven that they will generate enough revenue to pay that money back. Meta’s message to investors will likely be something along the lines of: “trust the process.” Meta up until recently had little to show for its AI spend, and is expected to report $41.1 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter and $9.4 billion negative free cash flows, which would mark its first cash flow negative quarter since 2012. While we're on the topic, here’s what else the Street is expecting: Revenue at $63.3 million, up 23% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share at $6.79, down 6.3% year over year. Meta unveiled Muse, its personal AI agent, on Sept 8, meaning we’ll get a peak at how the new product performed in the first few weeks. The app surpassed 5 million downloads in its first three weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by multiple outlets .Wall Street appeared hopeful, sending Meta rallying in the weeks after the launch. Muse, which has a furry mascot that’s equal parts cute and unsettling, is one of the first big consumer AI products. You give it the keys to your email and credit cards and it can do things that are the bane of our existence, like make dinner reservations or order more Tide Pods. That’s a bit of a different play than its peers, which have made big bets on AI as a tool for corporations eager to do more with less humans. The relationship between AI companies and corporations is starting to show cracks but its relationship with consumers over a subscription based service is still in its early innings. It’s ultimately unclear if Muse will be the cashcow it needs to be in order to justify the amount Meta has spent on AI. The economics of a subscription product is also very different to Meta’s lucrative advertising business. And, as my colleague Walter Hickey pointed out earlier, it takes AI competitors like Amazon being willing to play ball in order for this thing to work as advertised. As we wade into a big week for tech earnings, the questions on everybody’s mind is as follows: How much more money are you going to spend and or borrow? When is the thing you’re working on going to make money? In Meta’s case, it has a shiny new product to talk about which is a better position than most of its peers. While it very well may report positive early adoption data, it still has to prove the product will be worth the many billions of dollars spent on it.
